specPoints.text: understand that knowledge of the rate equations for the hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes can be used to provide evidence for S N 1 and S N 2 mechanisms for tertiary and primary halogenoalkane hydrolysis

primer.text: Halogenoalkane hydrolysis can be raced: silver nitrate catches each liberated halide the instant water frees it, so precipitate colours clock the C-X bond breaking. This note runs the 50-degree test-tube protocol and reads the white-cream-yellow speed ladder, fluoride's soluble silence included.

lessons.title: Timing hydrolysis with silver nitrate
lessons.opening: Hydrolysis rates can be raced: three test tubes at 50 degrees, ethanol plus acidified silver nitrate as the medium, a few drops of each halogenoalkane, and a stopwatch per tube. The first precipitate to show is the fastest hydrolysis.
keyPoints: Acidified aqueous silver nitrate measures the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes.
Three test tubes in a 50 oC water bath hold ethanol mixed with acidified silver nitrate.
A few drops of chloroalkane, bromoalkane and iodoalkane start three stopwatches.
The time for each silver halide precipitate to form ranks the hydrolysis rates.

low.restatement: Silver ions catch the halide ions the moment water liberates them, so precipitate appearance times are a clock for C-X bond breaking; the water bath holds temperature constant across the race.
low.analogy: Three runners (C-X bonds) untying knots at the same temperature; the judge (Ag+) raises a flag the instant each knot gives way.
low.examPointer: Quote the controlled variables: same bath temperature (50 oC), same solvent mixture, same drops - the comparison is only fair if these hold.

medium.restatement: Precipitation timing converts an invisible bond-breaking rate into a visible clock. The ethanol co-solvent dissolves the halogenoalkanes; the nitric acid suppresses interfering ions so only liberated halide precipitates.
medium.analogy: A smoke detector wired to each bond: the alarm (precipitate) sounds when enough halide smoke accumulates.
medium.examPointer: Name the medium 'ethanol and acidified silver nitrate' precisely - missing either component loses the method mark.

check.stem: The reagent that detects hydrolysis progress is

options.explanation: Ag+ precipitates liberated halide ions, timing the C-X bond breaking.
That reagent drives substitution, not this rate test.
Unrelated to halide detection here.
No acid-base endpoint is timed.

check.stem: The water bath temperature for the hydrolysis race is

options.explanation: The set bath keeps all three tubes at the same temperature.
The method specifies the warm bath.
Too hot for the set-up as specified.
Far below the specified bath.

check.stem: Ethanol is mixed into the test tubes because

options.text: It dissolves the halogenoalkanes into the reacting mixture
options.explanation: The co-solvent brings the organic substrate into contact with the aqueous silver nitrate.

options.text: It reacts with the halide ions
options.explanation: Ethanol takes no reacting part.

options.text: It speeds the silver nitrate's reaction
options.explanation: The silver chemistry is unaffected; ethanol only aids dissolving.
Precipitate colours come from the silver halides.

check.stem: A precipitate forms in these tubes because

options.text: Hydrolysis liberates halide ions that silver ions catch as insoluble silver halide
options.explanation: Ag+ + X- -> AgX(s) is the visible clock.
No such solidification occurs.

options.text: Silver nitrate reacts with the whole halogenoalkane directly
options.explanation: Silver reacts with liberated halide, not the intact C-X bond.

options.text: The water bath freezes the mixture
options.explanation: The bath warms, not freezes.

check.stem: Starting three stopwatches simultaneously matters because

options.text: The precipitate times must share a common start to rank the rates fairly
options.explanation: A common zero makes the three clocks comparable.
No such decomposition drives the timing.

options.text: The bath temperature changes every minute
options.explanation: The bath holds temperature steady.
They form gradually - that is the whole measurement.

check.stem: State the mixture held in each test tube.
check.modelAnswer: Ethanol mixed with acidified aqueous silver nitrate, plus a few drops of the halogenoalkane.

check.stem: State what is timed in each tube.
check.modelAnswer: The time taken for the silver halide precipitate to appear.

check.stem: Explain why faster precipitate formation indicates faster hydrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: Halide ions appear only as fast as the C-X bond breaks; silver catches them immediately, so the precipitate clock mirrors the hydrolysis rate.

check.stem: One tube's precipitate appears in 20 s, another's in 200 s. Which halogenoalkane is in the faster tube, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The 20 s tube holds the iodoalkane: its weak C-I bond breaks fastest, liberating iodide and precipitating silver iodide soonest.

lessons.title: The precipitate ladder and class comparisons
lessons.opening: The precipitates read like a traffic light: white silver chloride crawls, cream silver bromide middles, yellow silver iodide sprints - the C-I bond snaps first because it is weakest. Silver fluoride never shows, being soluble, and within one halogen the tertiary substrate hydrolyses quickest.
keyPoints: The yellow silver iodide precipitate marks the fastest nucleophilic substitution because the C-I bond surrenders at the lowest enthalpy of the series.
The white silver chloride precipitate marks the slowest, as C-Cl has the highest bond enthalpy.
Silver fluoride is soluble, so no precipitate forms for fluoroalkanes.
Comparing primary, secondary and tertiary with the same halogen shows tertiary hydrolysing quickest and primary slowest.

low.restatement: Precipitate colour and speed encode bond enthalpy: yellow-fast iodide, cream-mid bromide, white-slow chloride, nothing for fluoride. Same-halogen class races put tertiary first, primary last.
low.analogy: Three locks with different weaknesses: the rusty iodide lock opens instantly, the chloride lock barely yields, and the fluoride lock has no keyhole at all (soluble silver salt).
low.examPointer: Predict astatide as even quicker than iodide - one step further down the group's bond-enthalpy slide.

medium.restatement: Bond enthalpy governs the halogen trend while substrate class governs the same-halogen trend; the controlled comparison (1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane) varies only the carbon framework.
medium.analogy: One variable at a time: halogen for the colour ladder, carbon class for the speed ladder - the two ladders never share a rung.
medium.examPointer: The SN1/SN2 explanation of the class trend is A-level material; at AS, observe and order without mechanistic justification.

check.stem: Which silver halide precipitate appears fastest in the hydrolysis race?

options.explanation: The weakest C-I bond liberates iodide fastest.
The strongest C-Cl bond breaks slowest.
Bromide middles the ladder.
AgF is soluble - no precipitate forms at all.

check.stem: No precipitate forms for fluoroalkanes because

options.text: Silver fluoride is soluble in the reaction medium
options.explanation: No insoluble AgF can accumulate visibly.
They form; they simply stay dissolved with Ag+.
C-F is the strongest bond and reacts slowest or not at all.
AgF exists; it is just soluble.

check.stem: The order of halogenoalkane reactivity by halogen is

options.text: Iodoalkane > bromoalkane > chloroalkane, with fluoroalkane least
options.explanation: Bond enthalpy falls down the group, so reactivity rises.
That reverses the bond-enthalpy logic.
C-F is strongest, so fluoroalkanes are least reactive.

options.text: All equal, as each carries one halogen
options.explanation: The halogen identity changes the bond strength decisively.

check.stem: Comparing 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane hydrolysis rates, the fastest is

options.explanation: Tertiary hydrolyses quickest of the three classes.
Primary hydrolyses slowest here.
Secondary middles the class trend.
Class changes the rate even at fixed halogen.

check.stem: Which variables must stay constant in the primary-secondary-tertiary comparison?

options.text: The halogen stays the same and the overall formula does too
options.explanation: Both are named as the controls for the class comparison.

options.text: The halogen and the carbon class
options.explanation: The carbon class is the variable, not a control.

options.text: The water bath and the solvent only
options.explanation: Those matter too, but the named controls are halogen and formula.
Fair comparison requires the controls.

check.stem: State the colours and speed order of the three silver halide precipitates.
check.modelAnswer: White AgCl slowest, cream AgBr middle, pale yellow AgI fastest.

check.stem: State the prediction for silver astatide.
check.modelAnswer: Silver astatide would form even more quickly than silver iodide, one step further down the group.

check.stem: Explain why the C-I bond breaks fastest in hydrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: Of the carbon-halogen series the C-I bond surrenders at the lowest enthalpy, so least energy is needed to break it and iodide ions form first.

check.stem: A same-halogen race uses 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Predict the order and name the controlled variable that makes the race fair.
check.modelAnswer: The tertiary 2-bromo-2-methylpropane precipitates first, primary 1-bromobutane last; fairness requires the same halogen (bromine) and the same molecular formula C4H9Br in both tubes.

glossary.definition: The speed at which water breaks the C-X bond, measured by silver halide precipitation times.
The Ag+ reagent (with nitric acid) that precipitates liberated halide ions on sight.
The energy needed to break a bond; it falls from C-F to C-I, setting the hydrolysis order.
